Discover

Most expensive bugs are requirements bugs, not code bugs — I spend time scoping before I touch an editor, because a wrong assumption compounds with every hour spent building on top of it.

  • Stakeholder interview(surfaces the real constraint before it becomes a rewrite) — talk directly to whoever hits the problem today; their workaround usually tells you more than the ticket does.
  • Problem framing(keeps the team from building the wrong thing, well) — restate the ask as the outcome that should change, not the feature that was requested.
  • Constraint mapping(a design that ignores timeline, team, or data constraints doesn't ship) — write down what's actually fixed — deadline, existing schema, headcount — before proposing anything.
  • Acceptance criteria(gives "done" a testable definition on day one, not an argument on day thirty) — define the specific, verifiable conditions that prove the problem is solved, before writing any code.

In practice: On the event registration system, the original ask was "add a CSV export so admins can see who's registered." Talking to the admins who'd actually use it surfaced the real problem: the dashboard had no way to flag duplicate or conflicting registrations before an event, so they were catching those manually, after the fact, at check-in. The ticket became a real-time conflict view instead of an export button — a smaller build than requested, and the thing that actually fixed their recurring complaint.

Design

I'd rather spend an afternoon on a design doc than a week unwinding a bad data model in production — most hard bugs are architecture decisions nobody wrote down.

  • Design doc / RFC(forces trade-offs onto paper before they're load-bearing in code) — a short written proposal: the approach taken, the alternative considered, and why it lost.
  • API contract first(lets frontend and backend build in parallel against a stable shape) — agree on request/response shapes before either side writes implementation code.
  • Data modeling(the cost of a wrong schema compounds with every row written against it) — model around how data is actually queried, not just how it's created.
  • Trade-off analysis(keeps a team from re-implementing a problem someone already solved) — explicitly weigh consistency vs. availability, latency vs. simplicity, custom code vs. an existing library, before committing.

In practice: For the helpdesk management system, the key decision was how to model ticket ownership. The obvious approach — a single assigned_agent_id column on the ticket — was rejected because it couldn't represent reassignment or escalation history, which the support team needed for SLA auditing. Modeling assignment as its own table, separate from the ticket, cost one extra join on every read but meant escalations were just new rows, not destructive updates.

Build

Shipping in small, reviewable pieces is the single habit that's saved me the most time — a 2,000-line pull request is a pull request nobody actually reviews.

  • Small, reviewable PRs(a diff a reviewer can hold in their head catches more bugs than one they skim) — one logical change per pull request, not one feature spanning a dozen files.
  • Test-alongside development(catches a regression before a reviewer or a user does) — write the test for the behavior you just added in the same sitting, not as a follow-up ticket.
  • Code review(a second set of eyes catches the assumption you stopped noticing) — treat review comments as free bug reports, not as obstacles to merging.
  • Feature flags(decouples deploying code from releasing a feature) — ship the code dark, verify it in production, then flip it on — instead of a release day that's also the first real-world test.

In practice: Building checkout for the handmade-candle e-commerce site, I split what could've been one large "add checkout" change into separate pull requests — cart persistence, address capture, payment integration, order confirmation — each shippable on its own. That discipline paid off directly: a reviewer caught that a failed or cancelled payment wasn't handled before the order record was created, which would have left paid-looking orders in the database for carts that never actually completed.

Verify

"It works on my machine" isn't verification — I only consider something done once I can see it behaving correctly in production, not just in a test suite.

  • Testing pyramid(catches different classes of bugs at the cheapest layer that can catch them) — most coverage from fast unit tests, fewer but real integration tests, a thin layer of end-to-end tests for the critical paths.
  • Staging / canary deploys(limits the blast radius of a bad change before it reaches every user) — roll out to a subset of traffic or a pre-production environment first, and watch it before a full release.
  • Monitoring & observability(turns "it broke" into "here's exactly what broke and why") — instrument logs, metrics, and traces so a production issue is diagnosable from a dashboard, not from guesswork.
  • Rollback plan(makes a bad deploy a five-minute incident instead of a five-hour one) — know how to revert before you need to, not while an incident is already live.

In practice: On the event management system, the real test wasn't the staging environment — it was event day itself, a fixed deadline with a traffic spike right as doors opened. Rather than find out live, I load-tested the check-in flow specifically ahead of the event, which surfaced a slow query under concurrent check-ins that never showed up under normal day-to-day traffic. Fixed before the event, not during it.

Try it↗GitHub↗

Purpose

Developers kept stopping their own work to hand-write release notes and other JSON documents for the rest of the team. I built MyAML so the people who need those documents can produce valid JSON themselves.

Target audience

Business analysts, project managers and other non-technical staff who need structured JSON such as release notes, plus the developers or leads who design the reusable structures for them.

What it solves

  • Removes a developer bottleneck. Non-technical staff create release notes and other structured JSON themselves, so developers no longer write it by hand.
  • No JSON knowledge needed. Users fill in a normal form and the app writes valid, properly formatted JSON. There are no missing commas, unclosed brackets or broken quotes.
  • Plain-language data types. Fields are labelled "Text", "Whole number", "Yes/No", "Group", "List" and "Choice", each with a short example, instead of string, integer and boolean.
  • Ready-made release-notes template. The app opens with version, date, tasks and sub-tasks already set up, so the most common request works straight away.
  • Reusable structures. A developer or lead designs the structure once in the Blueprint tab, and anyone can fill it in from the Editor tab as often as needed.
  • Catches mistakes early. Empty required fields are flagged in the form and highlighted in the JSON preview, blank or duplicate field names are marked, and a status bar shows whether the output is valid.
  • Easy hand-off. One click copies the JSON or downloads it as a dated .json file, ready to send to the development team.

What I learned

  • Schema-driven dynamic forms. Built a form engine in Angular 20 with standalone components that builds itself from a user-defined schema, using a recursive template that handles objects inside arrays inside objects to any depth.
  • Reactive state with RxJS. Centralised state with BehaviorSubject and combineLatest keeps the Blueprint, the Editor and the live preview in sync.
  • Data-preserving schema changes. Renaming a field or changing its type keeps the values already entered instead of resetting them.
  • A custom JSON tokenizer. Powers the preview's line numbers, syntax colours and per-line error highlighting, with caching so it doesn't redo the work on every change.
  • Recursive algorithms. Used for validation, nesting-depth calculation and node counting in the status bar.
  • Theming with design tokens. A custom PrimeNG theme built from design tokens and SCSS variables, with a "developer terminal" look.
  • Accessibility in practice. Keyboard navigation between tabs, visible focus outlines, tooltips on icon-only buttons, reduced-motion support and a responsive phone layout.
  • Shipping the details. In-app release notes (the app uses the same kind of notes it helps produce), Angular Router routes, SEO metadata, and a move of the unit tests to Vitest.

Try it↗GitHub↗
Problem
A small handmade-candle business needed its own online store to sell directly to customers.
Constraints
Solo project, built in my own time for a friend's home business. I owned everything from database design to deployment, with no team to review my code, and the owner isn't technical, so managing products and orders had to be simple and hosting costs had to stay low.
Role
Full-stack: ASP.NET Core API with Dapper and SQL Server, and the React storefront.
Architecture
React storefront -> ASP.NET Core Web API -> Dapper -> SQL Server
Technical challenge
Handling failed or cancelled payments correctly, so an order record is never created for a cart that didn't actually complete checkout.
Decision
Split checkout into separately shippable pull requests — cart persistence, address capture, payment integration, order confirmation — instead of one large change, so each piece could be tested and shipped on its own while working solo. Chose Dapper over Entity Framework Core because the schema is small and checkout depends on a few critical queries. Writing that SQL by hand made it clear exactly when an order, its stock updates and its payment status are written in one transaction, and Dapper's low overhead suited cheap hosting.
Result
The business has its own storefront to sell directly to customers instead of relying only on word of mouth and social media messages. Reviewing my own payment-integration PR before merging caught the failed-payment case before release, so a declined or cancelled payment leaves the cart intact and never creates an order.
What I learned
Working alone doesn't mean skipping process: splitting checkout into small PRs and reviewing each one as if someone else wrote it is what caught the payment bug before a real customer could hit it.

About

I'm Shantanu, a backend-first full-stack developer based in Surat, Gujarat. My home ground is C#, ASP.NET Core Web API, Entity Framework Core and SQL Server, and I also build the Angular and React front ends that sit on top of those APIs, so I can take a feature from the database schema all the way to the screen.

I started in 2022 as an Angular intern at WeeTech Solution, turning UI/UX designs into responsive interfaces and wiring them to REST APIs. Later that year I joined ProjectTree as a Junior Software Engineer on ASP.NET MVC and Angular apps, and within a few months moved up to Full Stack Developer, the role I've held for over four years.

At ProjectTree I build enterprise applications that people use every day: an Event Registration System with real-time seat availability and payments, an Event Management Platform with scheduling and automated notifications, an internal HelpDesk with role-based ticket routing and SLA tracking, and Leave Management workflows that replaced manual approvals.

I treat performance and security as features rather than afterthoughts. Refactoring SQL Server queries and adding Redis caching cut our API response times by 40%, and JWT authentication, role-based authorization and secrets kept in HashiCorp Vault go in from the first commit. Builds and releases run through Jenkins and Azure DevOps pipelines, with Docker where it fits.

Beyond my own code, I mentor junior developers through code reviews and pair programming on .NET and Angular best practices. I'm certified in Claude Code, so AI-assisted development is part of my everyday workflow, and outside work I build side projects such as MyAML, a JSON config builder in Angular 20 that lets non-technical teams create valid config files from a simple form.

I enjoy clean, readable code, APIs that are fast and safe by default, and interfaces that just make sense. If you're looking for a .NET and Angular developer who cares about both ends of the stack, I'd love to hear from you.
